archetype.name: Playoff Team (ball-control, record a notch ahead of its play)
archetype.definition: A legitimately above-average team on both sides of the ball, top-ten in net efficiency, whose 7-2 record is still padded by close-game results and has survived a turnover margin that should have cost it more.

report.headline: Better than its turnovers, not quite as good as 7-2 says
report.take:
Ben Johnson's second Bears team is good, and the reasons are sturdy. They lead the league in time of possession at 34.52 minutes a game, sit third in yards per game, and the defense is the best in football on third down, allowing conversions just 22.8% of the time. Add a pass rush with 26 sacks (third) and special teams worth 3.23 EPA a game (fourth), and you get a team whose net EPA ranks ninth and whose point differential ranks seventh. It is a real playoff-caliber profile, and an upgrade on the defense from 2025, when it ranked 21st in EPA allowed.

The record, though, runs ahead of that profile. The point differential implies about five wins, not seven; Wins Over Expected credits them with two extra, fourth-most in the league, and they've won 75% of their one-score games. That is the second straight year of outrunning the scoreboard: 2025's 11-win team was also near the top of the league in Wins Over Expected. What makes this version odd is how it got there. Last year's luck came with a league-best turnover margin; this year they're 29th at -0.9 a game, with 17 giveaways against 13 takeaways. Two games with five giveaways each tell the story: one was the 31-7 loss in Green Bay with Tyson Bagent at quarterback, the other a 27-24 escape against Tampa Bay that only held because the defense took the ball back twice and sacked the quarterback four times.

The quarterback churn matters for reading the season. Caleb Williams started the first two games, missed three (Case Keenum won both of his starts, Bagent lost his badly), and has won every start since returning in Week 6. That stretch is the truer picture of this team: an offense that moves the ball with a balanced plan, a line that keeps the passer clean (sixth-lowest pressure rate allowed) despite the league's longest time to throw, and a defense that chokes off the short game, second in EPA on short passes. The flaw is the other end of the field. The Bears are dead last in EPA allowed on deep passes, and they're down a starting corner with another questionable.

Where it goes: the turnover margin is mostly noise and should drift toward even, which helps. The close-game magic is also noise and should fade, which hurts. Those roughly cancel, leaving a team that should win more than it loses. But the schedule after this week is brutal, with two Detroit games, Jacksonville, Buffalo, Green Bay and a finale in Minnesota, in a division where three teams sit at 7-2.

strengths.title: Third-down defense and the pass rush
strengths.body: Opponents convert only 22.8% of third downs, the best rate in the league, and that rests on a rush that sacks the quarterback on 8.6% of dropbacks (third) and a coverage shell that smothers short throws. A defense that wins the money down off the rush tends to hold up, because sacks and pressure are among the more stable defensive traits. The loss of DT Kentavius Street to IR thins the rotation, but he was a 41%-snap player.

strengths.title: Ball control that shortens games
strengths.body: Chicago holds the ball longer than anyone, sits eighth in offensive success rate and third in yards per game, and pairs a top-ten defense with fourth-ranked special teams. Sustained drives plus field position keep the defense fresh and the opponent's possessions few. With Williams back, this is a repeatable style rather than a fluke.

strengths.title: A clean pocket despite long holds
strengths.body: The line allows pressure on just 17.2% of dropbacks (sixth) and QB hits at the fifth-lowest rate, even though the Bears' quarterbacks hold the ball longer than anyone. That gives the offense time for the slower-developing concepts Johnson favors. Losing tackle Braxton Jones for the year tests that depth from here on.

concerns.title: A record the scoreboard doesn't fully back
concerns.body: Seven wins on a differential that implies five is the definition of a record running ahead of its play, and the 75% one-score win rate carries much of the gap. History says close-game records drift toward .500. That doesn't make this a bad team, but the margin for error against a hard back half is thinner than 7-2 suggests.

concerns.title: Giveaways in clumps
concerns.body: Seventeen turnovers through nine games leave them 29th in margin, and the damage comes in bursts: five in Green Bay, five more against Tampa Bay. Some of it was backup-quarterback chaos, but the Tampa game came with Williams under center. Turnovers are largely noise and should improve. Another five-giveaway game against a good opponent, though, is a loss.

concerns.title: The deep ball, now with corners hurt
concerns.body: The Bears allow more EPA on deep throws than any team in the league, and explosive passes get through at a bottom-third rate. That is the price of a scheme that squeezes everything short, and it's getting worse rather than better: Malik Muhammad is out and Tyrique Stevenson left the Tampa game with a hand injury. Good vertical offenses on the schedule (Buffalo, Detroit, Jacksonville) will test it.

trend.note: Since Williams returned in Week 6 the Bears have won every game, including a convincing 34-17 win at Seattle with positive EPA through the air and on the ground. The Tampa Bay game was a warning: negative passing EPA and five giveaways, saved by the defense. The bye week gives them a chance to reset.

nextGame.headline: Rested Bears get a Saints line missing three starters
nextGame.body:
Chicago comes off a bye with 14 days of rest to host a 3-6 New Orleans team that ranks 26th in net EPA, and the Book makes the Bears 11.5-point favorites. The matchup tilts hard toward Chicago on both lines of scrimmage. The Saints' defense is 31st in EPA against the run, 31st in pressure rate and 28th on third down, which suits an offense that wants to run, convert and hold the ball. Their offense under Tyler Shough runs poorly (31st in rush success) and leans pass, which runs straight into the Bears' best unit, the third-down pass rush. The one place New Orleans can hurt Chicago is downfield: the Bears are last in deep-pass EPA allowed.

Availability swings this further. The Saints are without right tackle Taliese Fuaga and center Erik McCoy, both near-every-snap starters, and Asim Richards is out for multiple weeks, so a battered line faces a rush with 26 sacks. Linebacker Pete Werner is questionable with a hamstring. On Chicago's side, Luther Burden (concussion) was practicing and Kyle Monangai is eyeing a return, but the secondary is the worry: Muhammad is out and Stevenson is questionable. The early forecast calls for sustained wind in the mid-teens with stronger gusts. It's days out and could change, but if it holds it would push the game toward the run and make Chicago's ground plan even more central.

waysToWin.title: Rush a patchwork Saints line
waysToWin.body: With Fuaga and McCoy out and Richards sidelined, New Orleans is starting backups at multiple spots against a defense that sacks quarterbacks at the third-best rate in the league. Shough has been the Saints' only starter, and pressure forces the long-yardage downs where Chicago is the best team in football. Drive-killing sacks also keep the deep shots that worry this secondary off the table.

waysToWin.title: Run and keep the ball
waysToWin.body: The Saints rank 31st in EPA against the run and 28th on third down, and the Bears lead the league in time of possession. Leaning on D'Andre Swift, possibly with Monangai back, keeps Chicago ahead of the chains, shortens the game and protects a thin secondary. A windy afternoon would only strengthen the case.

waysToWin.title: Feed Loveland and the top receiver
waysToWin.body: New Orleans has been soft on tight ends, 28th in EPA allowed to opponents' TE1, and lets WR1s score well above their usual output. Colston Loveland is the second-most targeted Bear, and Burden leads the team if he clears the concussion protocol. Those are the targets to build the passing game around.

waysToLose.title: Turnovers hand back short fields
waysToLose.body: The Bears' giveaways come in bunches, and a five-turnover day like the Tampa game would give a weak Saints offense short fields it can't earn on its own. That is the most realistic path to an upset. New Orleans ranks only 20th in takeaways, so this one is mostly on Chicago.

waysToLose.title: Shots over a depleted secondary
waysToLose.body: Chicago is last in deep-pass EPA allowed and is missing at least one starting corner. The Saints pass more than expected and need only a few explosive plays to stay in range. If the rush doesn't get home first, that's where points come from.

waysToLose.title: Long holds meet a finishing rush
waysToLose.body: The Saints rarely pressure, but when they do they finish: their sack rate ranks fifth. The Bears' quarterbacks hold the ball longer than anyone, and the line just lost Braxton Jones for the year. Drive-killing sacks would stall the possession game Chicago needs.

nextGame.watch: Chicago's edge rush against New Orleans' backup tackles and center: early sacks turn this into a rout, while a clean pocket for Shough brings the Bears' deep-ball weakness into play.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the Bears to stay good but win at a less charmed rate. The efficiency is real: top-ten net EPA, the best third-down defense, a strong pass rush, a clean pocket and ball control. The turnover margin should drift toward even, which will help, but the close-game luck that put them two wins above their differential will likely fade. The bigger issue is the schedule. After New Orleans and Miami, almost every remaining opponent is a winning team, including Detroit twice, Jacksonville, Buffalo on the road and a closing trip to Minnesota's top-ranked defense.

A realistic finish lands around the low double digits in wins, with the division decided in those four NFC North games. The deep-pass defense and the health of the corners will decide whether they hold up against Detroit, Buffalo and Jacksonville. Williams's ball security decides most of the rest.
swingFactors: Results in the four division games

confidence.note: Nine games across three starting QBs, plus heavy turnover and close-game noise.
